design_detail: Subgroup meta-analyses of the 107 prospective cohort studies of alcohol and all-cause mortality assembled for the same group's earlier review (Zhao et al., 2023: the 87 studies of Stockwell et al., 2016, plus 20 added; search to 31 July 2021). Studies were grouped by characteristics predicted by the authors' theory of lifetime selection bias (Naimi et al., 2017) to make low-volume drinkers look healthier than abstainers: primarily a median cohort age of 55 or younger at enrolment (with follow-up to at least 56) and no former or occasional drinkers in the abstainer reference group, secondarily an intake measure covering at least 30 days, exclusion of people with prior illness, and control for smoking and for socio-economic status (SES). Low-volume intake (1.30 to under 25 g ethanol a day) against abstainers was pooled by mixed-effects regression of log relative risks with a random study effect (SAS PROC MIXED), preceded by bivariate comparisons of mean relative risks between study subgroups (Table 1). Presented as a response to a critique of Zhao et al. (2023) by the International Scientific Forum on Alcohol Research (ISFAR). Protocol described as preregistered on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/tnhd3; not read).
can_establish: How the pooled relative risk of death for low-volume drinking (1.30 to under 25 g a day) against abstainers differs between subgroups of published cohort studies defined by cohort age and by whether former and occasional drinkers were counted as abstainers, and how few published cohorts meet both criteria.
cannot_establish: Whether low-volume drinking lowers, raises or does not change mortality (pooled observational cohorts; restriction does not remove confounding); whether the difference between subgroups is caused by the biases named rather than by other features of the studies (a study-level comparison, six unnamed studies in the decisive subgroup, no test of the difference reported); the shape of risk within the 1.30 to 25 g range; or anything firm about nonsmokers (an exploratory, unadjusted mean of six studies for one intake category).

sample.recruitment: Review-level: PubMed and Web of Science for articles published up to 31 July 2021, with reference lists of earlier meta-analyses checked; the search and flowchart belong to Zhao et al. (2023) and the supplement (Figure A2, not read). The cohorts came from North and Central America (40 studies), Europe and Australia (48) and Asia (12) (Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English-language original research in peer-reviewed journals; prospective cohort studies relating at least two levels of alcohol consumption to all-cause mortality in general populations of any age. Excluded: reviews, letters, editorials, commentaries, unpublished work, dissertations, government reports, books, conference proceedings and meeting abstracts, guidelines; cohorts selected for a specific illness or for heavy, problematic or dependent drinking. Where several publications came from one data set, the most recent was coded unless populations differed (Method › Inclusion and exclusion criteria; Data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Study level only: median cohort age at baseline 19 to 55 in 61 studies and 56 to 78 in 44; result sets for men only (66), women only (45) and both sexes (29), counts overlapping because some studies report by sex (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the primary cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English only, peer-reviewed only, two databases, no grey literature; the search closed three years before publication. The decisive subgroup holds six or seven studies that are not named in the main text, with no count of their participants or deaths. The grouping variables come from the authors' own theory, and the paper responds to a critique of the authors' previous analysis of the same studies.

exposure.measurement: Baseline self-reported intake as each cohort measured it, over periods from 2 or 3 days to a lifetime, converted to grams of ethanol a day from category midpoints; open top categories were set at the lower bound plus three quarters of the width of the next category down. Where a study did not define its drink, national sizes were assumed: 8 g (United Kingdom), 10 g (Australia, Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Netherlands, New Zealand, Poland, Spain, Sweden), 11 g (Finland), 12 g (Denmark, Germany, Italy, South Africa, Switzerland and other countries), 12.5 g (China), 13.45 g (Canada), 14 g (United States), 19.75 g (Japan). Only 27 of 99 studies measured typical intake over at least 30 days (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories (g ethanol a day): former drinkers; occasional, under 1.30 (up to one 10-g drink a week); low volume, 1.30 to under 25 (up to two drinks); medium, 25 to under 45; higher, 45 or more (Tables 2 and 3; printed bounds vary, reporting issues 1 to 3). Lifetime abstainers: never one drink; current drinkers: at least one 10-g drink in the past year (p. 443).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking handled only as a study characteristic: 83 studies controlled for it by adjustment or stratification and 18 did not; 6 reported results for nonsmokers and 7 for smokers (Table 1). Other drugs not addressed.

comparison.controls: Abstainers as defined by each cohort, coded for contamination: both former and occasional drinkers counted as abstainers (46 of 99 studies), former drinkers only (27), occasional drinkers only (8), neither (18). 'Neither' requires a strict lifetime-abstainer reference: never one drink, with any occasional lifetime or past-year drinking (for example fewer than 12 drinks, or 'rarely') disqualifying; studies measuring usual drinking over a week or a month were assumed to include occasional drinkers among their abstainers (pp. 442-443; Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Lifetime drinking histories, health-related reductions in drinking before baseline, and the ways lifetime abstainers differ from drinkers (health, religion, socio-economic position) are not available at review level; restricting to lifetime-abstainer reference groups removes former drinkers from the comparison but not these other differences.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking in the reference groups not reported.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality: hazard ratios and rate ratios used as relative risks; where only mortality rates were reported they were converted to relative risks; estimates were re-referenced to abstainers where needed (Method › Data extraction, Outcomes).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death ascertainment as in each cohort (not described).
outcomes.operationalization: A 'health benefit' is a relative risk below 1 for low-volume drinkers against the abstainer reference group.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, but Table 1 reports 17 bivariate p values and Tables 2 and 3 report 15 pooled estimates, each in two model versions, all judged at p < .05 (bold in the tables).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Three coders extracted and coded each study independently, resolving disagreements with the principal investigator and investigators (Method › Data extraction, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Low volume (1.30 to under 25 g a day) against abstainers, random study effect ('adjusted' for between-study variation), with the estimate without it ('partially adjusted') second (Table 3): all 107 studies 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88) and 0.85 (0.82 to 0.88), 99 studies, 306 estimates; older cohorts 0.84 (0.81 to 0.87); both abstainer biases 0.85 (0.81 to 0.89); older cohorts with both biases 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), 18 studies; plus a poor intake measure 0.83 (0.77 to 0.90), 15 studies; younger cohorts only 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92), 51 studies; no abstainer bias only 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95), 18 studies; younger cohorts and no abstainer bias 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) and 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24), 6 studies, 38 estimates; plus a 30-day measure 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) and 1.14 (1.00 to 1.29), 5 studies. Higher-quality subgroup, other categories against lifetime abstainers (Table 2, random effect): former drinkers 1.32 (1.13 to 1.54); medium 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40); higher, 45 g or more, 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82). Bivariate unadjusted means (Table 1): younger 0.93 vs older 0.83 (p = .0085); poor health excluded or controlled 0.97 vs not 0.84 (p = .0004); 30-day measure 0.99 vs 0.86 (p = .0026); neither abstainer bias 0.99 vs both 0.82 (p = .0004); no smoking control 1.01 vs control 0.86 (p = .0010); no SES control 0.97 vs control 0.85 (p = .0010); nonsmokers 1.16 (0.91 to 1.41) vs smokers 0.93 (0.71 to 1.16) (p = .1817). No heterogeneity statistic, prediction interval or absolute rate is reported. Editors' calculation: ratio of the higher-quality (0.98) to the lower-quality (0.84) subgroup estimate 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), z = 2.23, p of about .03, treating the two disjoint sets of studies as independent.
analysis.covariates: None at review level beyond the random study effect: 'adjusted' in Tables 2 and 3 means adjusted for between-study variation, not for confounders. Covariates differ between the primary studies; whether the most-adjusted estimate of each study was used is not stated here (methods referred to Zhao et al., 2023).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework, osf.io/tnhd3 (Stockwell et al., 2021), not read. The paper says the two primary criteria (cohort age, abstainer bias) are those of the preregistered protocol and calls the smoking and SES analyses exploratory; it does not say whether the intake-measure and baseline-illness criteria or the nonsmoker analysis were registered, nor whether the registration preceded the search (which closed on 31 July 2021). Zhao et al. (2023) have a different registration (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G, according to card sc_zhao_2023).
analysis.selective_reporting: Absent from the main text: heterogeneity statistics, the names and sizes of the decisive studies, a test of the difference between higher- and lower-quality subgroups, and any check for publication bias. Medium and higher categories for the lower-quality studies appear only in Figure 2; the contrast of 5 against 15 studies (Figure B5) and the forest plots (Figures B1 to B4) are in the supplement (not read).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The decisive subgroup has 6 studies and 38 estimates; its interval (0.87 to 1.11) runs from a 13% lower to an 11% higher risk. The authors say more higher-quality studies are needed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the 6 cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger and using lifetime abstainers as the reference, low-volume drinkers (1.30 to under 25 g a day) had an RR of 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), and 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without the random study effect; former drinkers (1.32) and people drinking 45 g a day or more (1.51) had higher mortality. Cohorts meeting neither criterion gave 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), and cohorts meeting only one criterion 0.88. In bivariate, unadjusted comparisons, cohorts that controlled for smoking or SES showed lower low-volume RRs than those that did not, and the six cohorts reporting nonsmokers separately gave 1.16 (0.91 to 1.41) for nonsmokers against 0.93 for smokers (p = .18).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports that the higher-quality studies estimated "similar mortality risk for low-volume drinkers" as abstainers and that RRs in nonsmoking cohorts were above 1.0 (p. 441); the Discussion says the findings support lifetime selection biases creating the false appearance of benefit (p. 448); the Conclusions say that studies of nonsmokers find no J-shaped curve (p. 450). Gaps: (1) the decisive estimate rests on 6 unnamed studies whose participants and deaths are not counted, and its interval is compatible with a 13% lower risk; (2) no test of the difference between higher- and lower-quality subgroups is reported in the main text (the editors' calculation gives p of about .03), and the comparison is between groups of studies, which differ in more than the two criteria: cohorts recruited at younger ages, even if followed to 56, contribute deaths at ages and from causes different from older cohorts, and lifetime abstainers differ from drinkers in other ways, so the difference is consistent with, but not specific to, the selection bias named; (3) the nonsmoker statement rests on an exploratory, unadjusted mean of six studies, not restricted by the quality criteria as far as the paper says, for one intake category, so no curve was estimated and the interval includes 0.91; (4) the suggestion that adjustment for smoking or SES creates the J-curve comes from comparing studies that did or did not adjust, which differ in other ways; the paper presents it as a question for future research, but the Conclusions state the nonsmoker finding as a result. The main estimate itself is reported accurately, with its interval, and the Discussion states the main limits.

timeline.event: Fillmore et al.: meta-analysis grouping cohort studies by abstainer definition and analysing higher-quality studies separately; this paper follows its definitions (Stockwell is a co-author, according to the reference list).
Di Castelnuovo et al.: J-shaped meta-analysis of 34 cohorts, not cited by this paper; the project list pairs them (card sc_di_castelnuovo_2006, this round).
Stockwell et al.: 87-study review whose studies and codebook are reused here (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round).
Naimi et al.: the authors' theory of lifetime selection biases, which this paper tests; Zhao et al.: CHD mortality meta-analysis described here as finding younger cohorts less prone to bias.
Wood et al.: pooled analysis restricted to current drinkers, which avoids the abstainer reference group; not cited here (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Ortolá et al.: older Spanish cohort in which apparent protection vanished when lifetime drinking was taken into account (as described here, p. 442; among the 20 added studies).
Open Science Framework protocol, osf.io/tnhd3 (Stockwell et al., 2021), not read.
Zhao et al.: the 107-study review with study-level adjustment; low-volume RR 0.93 there against 0.98 here (p. 446) (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).

ISFAR Critique 264 of Zhao et al. (web critique, not read), described by the authors as coming from a group with significant ties to the alcohol industry (citing a blog post by Siegel, 2023); Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health final report (Paradis et al., 2023), co-authored by Naimi and Sherk and cited here for the view that mortality cohorts are too bias-prone to ground guidelines.

Stockwell, Zhao and Naimi, reply to ISFAR (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 85:133-135), cited as the fuller response (not read); Stockley, Hendriks and Ellison, ISFAR's rejoinder (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 85:136-140), listed on PubMed as a comment on Zhao et al. according to card sc_zhao_2023 (not read).
This paper (received 10 September 2023, revised 22 January 2024; July 2024 issue). No correction is mentioned in the PDF; the reference record's retraction check is clear.

replication.where_it_stands: The third analysis by one group of an overlapping set of studies (Stockwell et al., 2016: 87 studies; Zhao et al., 2023: 107; this paper: subgroups of the same 107), so the three are not independent confirmations. That very few published cohorts both recruit before age 56 and use lifetime abstainers as the reference, and that these few show no lower mortality at 1.30 to under 25 g a day, stands as reported; whether the gap from other cohorts is caused by selection bias is argued between the authors and ISFAR (exchange not read). Claims should cite 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) with its six-study basis and lifetime-abstainer reference, alongside the individual-participant (Wood et al., 2018) and Mendelian randomization studies carded in this round.

funding.funder: Partly funded by the Canadian Centre of Substance Use and Addiction (so spelled in the footnote) as part of a contract to assist with the development of the new Canadian Guidance on Alcohol and Health (p. 441, footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: Stockwell, Sherk and Naimi declare previous funding from government alcohol monopolies in Finland, Sweden and Canada to conduct public-health-oriented alcohol research; Stockwell and Naimi also received personal fees from these bodies in the past for the same purposes, and travel support from IOGT-NTO, described as a not-for-profit non-governmental organization that advocates against alcohol use, to prepare reports on alcohol and health (Conflict-of-Interest Statement, p. 450).
funding.affiliations_note: Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research, University of Victoria (Stockwell, Zhao, Clay, Sherk, Naimi), Dalhousie University (Clay) and the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (Levesque, Sanger), which is also the funder. Naimi and Sherk are co-authors of the Canadian guidance report the contract supported (Paradis et al., 2023, reference list). The authors wrote the theory tested here and the two earlier reviews of the same studies, and the paper answers a critique of their own previous analysis. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant analysis of cohorts recruited in early adulthood with repeated, lifetime measures of drinking, comparing low-volume drinkers with lifetime abstainers and with stable occasional drinkers, reporting cause-specific deaths and absolute rates under a pre-specified adjustment set; genetic analyses able to estimate risk at low intake would test the same question without the abstainer reference group.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: General-population cohorts, intake in grams a day by category, abstainers (with their contamination coded) as comparator, all-cause mortality.

Provisional: the paper cites an OSF protocol (osf.io/tnhd3, 2021) and says the two primary criteria come from it, but the registration was not read, so its content, its timing relative to the search (closed 31 July 2021) and any deviations cannot be checked.
The question is about why some cohort studies find benefits, so cohorts are the designs at issue.

Two databases with keywords printed and reference lists, but English and peer-reviewed publications only without justification, no grey literature or registries, and a search closed three years before publication (project reading of item 4, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Provisional: selection is not described in the article, which refers to Zhao et al. (2023) and to the supplement flowchart (Figure A2), not read.
Three coders extracted and coded each study independently, disagreements resolved with the investigators (Method › Data extraction, 1st paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list in the article; the supplement contents the article names (Figures A1, A2, B1 to B5; Tables A1, A2) include a flowchart but no list of excluded studies; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article describes no study individually, not even the six that decide the main result; Table A1 (supplement, not read) lists the 20 added studies and Figures B1 to B4 hold forest plots.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No formal tool, but every study was coded for the selection and confounding problems at issue (abstainer contamination, cohort age, baseline illness, intake measure, control for smoking and SES); outcome ascertainment and selective reporting were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Inverse-variance-weighted mixed models of log relative risks with a random study effect, reported beside the fixed version. Met on balance, a close call: whether the most-adjusted primary estimates were used is not stated, crude rates were converted and pooled with adjusted ratios, correlation between estimates sharing a reference group is handled only by the random effect, and the Table 1 means appear to be computed on the untransformed scale (reporting issue 8).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The paper's purpose: pooled estimates are compared across subgroups defined by the bias-related characteristics (Tables 1 to 3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Results are interpreted through the bias subgroups, and the Discussion names residual problems in the higher-quality studies (the 55-year cut-off, former drinkers not reallocated).
Sources of between-study variation are the subject of the analysis and are discussed, although no Q or I2 value is reported despite the Methods (reporting issue 5).
Not mentioned for any subgroup; according to card sc_zhao_2023 the parent review ran funnel plots and Egger tests on the full pool.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding footnote and conflict-of-interest statement printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are 'no' (4, 7 and 15), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence whatever the provisional items (2, 5 and 8) turn out to be. The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not the value of the question: grouping studies by the features that could bias the abstainer comparison is a reasonable design, and the authors report the main estimate with its interval and state its limits. The practical consequences: the decisive estimate rests on six unnamed studies, heterogeneity and publication bias are unexamined, and the subgroup contrast is a comparison between groups of studies. The paper may be cited for the RR of 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) in younger cohorts with lifetime-abstainer references and for how rarely published cohorts meet those criteria; not for the claim that nonsmokers show no J-curve, nor as proof that the protective association is wholly bias.

key_findings.finding: Study pool: the 107 prospective cohort studies of alcohol and all-cause mortality assembled for Zhao et al. (2023): 87 from Stockwell et al. (2016) and 20 added, found by searching PubMed and Web of Science for articles published up to 31 July 2021 plus reference lists; English-language, peer-reviewed, general-population cohorts. The abstract gives 724 risk estimates, 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths; 99 studies gave estimates for low-volume drinking (306 estimates).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Method; Method › Overview; Search strategy for relevant studies, 1st paragraph; Inclusion criteria (p. 442); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 444); Table 3, row 'All 107 studies' (p. 447)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Exposure definitions: grams of ethanol a day at baseline; occasional drinkers under 1.30 g a day (up to one 10-g drink a week); low volume 1.30 to under 25 g a day (up to two drinks); medium 25 to under 45; higher 45 or more. Where a study did not define its drink, national sizes from 8 g (United Kingdom) to 19.75 g (Japan) were assumed (10 g for Australia, New Zealand and nine European countries, 13.45 g Canada, 14 g United States). Lifetime abstainers: never one drink; former drinkers: stopped completely by baseline; studies measuring usual drinking over a week or a month were assumed to include occasional drinkers among their abstainers.
key_findings.locator: Inclusion criteria, last bullet (p. 443); Method › Data extraction: Measures of alcohol consumption; Drinking categories; Misclassification of former and occasional drinkers as abstainers, both paragraphs (p. 443); Tables 2 and 3 row labels (p. 447)
key_findings.note: The printed bounds of the categories are inconsistent (reporting issues 1 to 3); grams a day as in Tables 2 and 3 should be used.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Quality criteria and how many studies meet them: of the 99 studies with low-volume estimates, 18 had neither former nor occasional drinkers among their abstainers, 46 had both, 27 former drinkers only and 8 occasional drinkers only; 27 measured typical intake over at least 30 days and 72 did not; 83 controlled for smoking (18 did not), 65 for SES (35 did not), and 44 excluded or controlled for poor health (56 did not). The primary criteria, said to be those of the preregistered protocol, were a median cohort age of 55 or younger at enrolment (with follow-up to at least 56) and no abstainer bias.
key_findings.locator: Method › Criteria for selecting studies of higher or lower quality for separate meta-analyses, items (a) to (f) and last paragraph (p. 444); Table 1 (p. 445)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Main result: in the 6 studies (38 estimates) with a median baseline age of 55 or younger, followed beyond 55, and with neither former nor occasional drinkers among the abstainers, low-volume drinkers (1.30 to under 25 g a day) had an RR for all-cause death of 0.98 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.11) against lifetime abstainers with a random study effect, and 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without it. With a 30-day intake measure required as well (5 studies, 34 estimates): 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15), and 1.14 (1.00 to 1.29; p = .047) without the random effect.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 444, continuing on p. 445) and 5th paragraph (p. 445, continuing on p. 446); Table 3, higher-quality rows, and Table 2, row 'Lower' (p. 447)
key_findings.note: The studies are not named and their participants and deaths are not counted in the main text; forest plots are in supplement Figures B1 to B4 (not read). 'Adjusted' in the tables means adjusted for between-study variation, not for confounders.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Other intake categories in the higher-quality subgroup (up to 7 studies), against lifetime abstainers with the random study effect: former drinkers RR 1.32 (1.13 to 1.54; 7 studies, 20 estimates); medium, 25 to under 45 g a day, 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40; 6 studies); higher, 45 g or more, 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82; 7 studies); all current drinkers 1.08 (0.95 to 1.25); all drinkers including former drinkers 1.23 (0.95 to 1.58). Without the random effect, every category except the lowest was significantly above 1 (for example medium 1.30, 1.05 to 1.60).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full
key_findings.note: Whether the 25 to under 45 g category is raised depends on the model: 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40) with the random study effect, 1.30 (1.05 to 1.60) without it, so 'higher death rates from 45 g a day' is a category boundary, not an estimated threshold; the authors add that their categories are too broad to locate where risk rises (key finding 10).

key_findings.finding: Lower-quality and single-criterion subgroups (low volume, random study effect): all 107 studies 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88; 99 studies, 306 estimates); median cohort age 56 or older 0.84 (0.81 to 0.87; 44 studies); both abstainer biases 0.85 (0.81 to 0.89; 46 studies); older cohorts with both biases 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89; 18 studies, 33 estimates); and with a poor intake measure as well 0.83 (0.77 to 0.90; 15 studies). Meeting one criterion only: cohorts aged 55 or younger 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92; 51 studies); no abstainer bias 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95; 18 studies).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 445, continuing on p. 446); Table 3 (p. 447)
key_findings.note: No test of the difference between the higher-quality (0.98) and lower-quality (0.84) subgroups is reported in the main text. Editors' calculation from the printed intervals, treating the two disjoint sets of studies as independent: ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), p of about .03.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Across intake categories (Figure 2, random study effect), the 6 higher-quality studies rise from low to medium to higher intake (0.98, 1.17, 1.51 in Table 2), while the curve of the 18 lower-quality studies stays at or below about 1, dipping at low volume; editors' reading of Figure 2 (approximate): about 0.83 (low; 0.84, 0.79 to 0.89, in Table 3 for the same 18 studies), 0.89 (medium) and 1.03 (45 g or more, interval about 0.95 to 1.11), so that in the lower-quality studies even the highest intake category was not clearly associated with higher mortality than in their abstainer groups.
key_findings.note: Values for the 18 lower-quality studies at medium and higher intake are read from the figure (approximate); they are not tabulated.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Bivariate comparisons (Table 1, 'unadjusted mean RR' for low volume, p for the subgroup difference): cohorts with median age 19 to 55, 0.93, against 56 to 78, 0.83 (p = .0085); poor health excluded or controlled 0.97 against not 0.84 (p = .0004); 30-day intake measure 0.99 against 0.86 (p = .0026); neither abstainer bias 0.99 against both 0.82 (p = .0004; former only 0.92 and occasional only 0.89, not significant); no control for smoking 1.01 against control 0.86 (p = .0010); no control for SES 0.97 against control 0.85 (p = .0010). Men-only, women-only and mixed result sets (0.88, 0.95, 0.85) and world regions did not differ significantly.
key_findings.note: These means are computed differently from the meta-analytic estimates of Tables 2 and 3 (reporting issue 8): on Table 3's method the no-abstainer-bias subgroup gives 0.88, not 0.99.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Smoking strata: in 6 studies reporting results for nonsmokers, the low-volume mean RR was 1.16 (0.91 to 1.41; 22 estimates), against 0.93 (0.71 to 1.16; 27 estimates) in 7 studies reporting smokers; the difference was not significant (p = .1817). The analysis is described as exploratory and comes from Table 1's unadjusted means.

key_findings.finding: Excluding studies at risk of bias, rather than adjusting for study characteristics as Zhao et al. (2023) did, gave a higher low-volume RR: 0.98 against 0.93 in Zhao et al.; the authors call the two approaches broadly consistent.

key_findings.finding: The authors' own caveats: neither criterion alone removes the biases (the 55-year cut-off is quite high, and abstainer bias cannot be fully corrected unless former drinkers are reallocated to drinking groups); very few studies meet the criteria and more are needed; many cohorts measured drinking over the previous week or only 2 or 3 days; the bivariate analyses control one characteristic at a time; and the low, medium and higher categories are too broad to locate the intake at which risk rises significantly.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 446, continuing on p. 447); 8th paragraph (p. 448, continuing on pp. 449-450)

key_findings.finding: The Conclusions state that biased abstainer reference groups can consistently create apparent benefits, that the few studies meeting minimal quality criteria show no significantly lower risk for low-volume drinkers, that studies of nonsmokers find no J-shaped curve, and that future research should test whether adjustment for smoking or SES makes low-volume drinkers look healthier than current abstainers.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

key_findings.finding: Background (the authors' description of other studies): the GBD 2020 estimate (Bryazka et al., 2022) is said to have assumed protection against ischaemic heart disease up to nine drinks a day and to have given 1.8 million alcohol-attributable deaths in 2020, about 1 million fewer than the GBD 2016 estimate (Griswold et al., 2018).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; check against cards sc_bryazka_2022 and sc_griswold_2018 before citing.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf (published version, J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024;85(4):441-452), read in full

reporting_issues.issue: The bounds of the low-volume category are printed differently in different places: more than 1.30 to under 25 g a day (abstract), 1.3 to 24 g (Method › Overview), 1.30 to 24 g (Drinking categories), 1.35 to 25 g (Results, 2nd paragraph), 1.30 to under 25 g (Tables 1 to 3) and 1.30 to 24 g (Figure 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables' 1.30 to under 25 g a day should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The occasional-drinker cut-off is given as up to one 10-g drink a week, under 1.30 g a day; one 10-g drink a week is 1.43 g a day (editors' arithmetic). The drink sizes implied by the other categories also vary (two drinks for 25 g, four for 45 g, six for 65 g).
reporting_issues.consequence: Category labels in drinks are approximate; claims should use grams a day.

reporting_issues.issue: The high-volume category is printed as up to 6 drinks or 25 to 64 g a day, overlapping the medium category (25 to 44 g); the analysed category in Tables 2 and 3 is 45 g a day or more.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typographical error for 45 to 64 g; no effect on the tabulated results.

reporting_issues.issue: The age criterion is described as a mean cohort age of 55 or younger, followed up beyond 55 (abstract); a median age at enrolment of up to 55, followed to at least 56 (Method, item b); followed until over 55 (Table 2 note); and followed up to at least 55 (Table 3 note).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Method's median age with follow-up to at least 56 is presumably what was applied.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I2 and that mixed models were used because significant heterogeneity was detected, but no Q, I2, tau-squared or prediction interval is reported for any pooled estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: How consistent the six decisive studies were with one another cannot be judged from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Table 2 presents outcomes for six studies, while Table 2 lists 7 studies for all drinkers, former drinkers, current drinkers and the highest category and 6 for the low and medium categories; neither the six nor the seven studies are named in the main text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup has 7 studies, 6 with low-volume estimates; the decisive studies can be identified only from the supplement's forest plots (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 51 of 97 studies as 52.28%; 51/97 is 52.58%, and the printed percentages of that panel sum to 99.71% (editors' arithmetic).

Table 1's 'unadjusted mean RR' intervals are symmetric on the untransformed scale (for example 1.16, 0.91 to 1.41; 0.89, 0.74 to 1.04), unlike the log-scale intervals of Tables 2 and 3 and the log-scale method described in the Methods; and Table 1's means for the same subgroups differ from Table 3's (cohorts aged 55 or younger, 51 studies and 169 estimates: 0.93 against 0.88; no abstainer bias, 18 studies and 78 estimates: 0.99 against 0.88).
reporting_issues.consequence: The bivariate comparisons, including the nonsmoker estimate quoted in the abstract, come from a computation the Methods do not describe; on the meta-analytic method the subgroup without abstainer bias still shows a significantly lower risk (0.88), as the Discussion acknowledges.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results contrast the higher-quality (0.98) and lower-quality (0.84) subgroups as if they differed, but no test of the difference is given in the main text; the supplement's Figure B5 (5 against 15 studies) is said to show significantly greater risk in the higher-quality studies at each level.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editors' calculation from the printed intervals gives p of about .03 (ratio 1.17, 1.02 to 1.34), so the contrast is nominally significant but not strongly so.

reporting_issues.issue: One of the 20 added studies, Kaprio et al. (2019), is cited as European Neuropsychopharmacology 29, S804, a supplement page of the kind used for congress abstracts, with a DOI carrying the year 2017; meeting abstracts are an exclusion criterion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a meeting abstract included against the stated criteria; one study of 107, and whether it is among the decisive studies is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Lifetime abstention is defined in the text as never drinking one drink, and in the Table 1 note as never having drunk more than one drink.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor ambiguity in the reference-group definition that decides the main result.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results (1st paragraph) list 'assessed alcohol use over less than 30 days' among the study characteristics with significantly higher low-volume relative risks, but Table 1 gives the higher relative risk to studies whose intake measure covered at least 30 days (0.99, 0.92 to 1.05, against 0.86, 0.82 to 0.90; p = .0026), and the Discussion lists measures covering less than 30 days among the characteristics that go with lower risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 and the Discussion agree, so the Results sentence is the error; claims should cite Table 1.
